title: Med Spa Appointment Buffer Time: How Much to Add (2026)
summary: How much med spa appointment buffer time to add between treatments, by service type, and how to set it so online booking cannot squeeze into the gap.
body_markdown:
## What Buffer Time Is and What It Protects


Buffer time is reserved calendar time after (or before) an appointment that no one can book into. It covers the work that happens between patients: wiping down the room, charting the visit, logging units used, restocking, and letting the provider breathe. Without it, a single 10-minute overrun cascades through the whole afternoon.


Scheduling vendors describe the mechanism in much the same way.[Arketa's help center](https://help.arketa.com/appointments/availability/buffers) explains that buffers pad a service so the calendar blocks the extra time while the client only sees the appointment length.[Pabau](https://support.pabau.com/en/pabau2/how-to-set-up-and-use-buffer-time-between-bookings) creates a block-out right after each new appointment. The idea is identical across tools; the difference is whether yours attaches it to the service or leaves it to staff memory.


## How Much Buffer Time Per Service


Start at 10 to 15 minutes for injectables and consults, 15 to 20 for laser and other room-heavy services, and zero to five for quick rechecks. Published guidance is a range, not a standard:[Prospyr's scheduling guide](https://prospyrmed.com/blog/post/time-slot-optimization-tips-med-spas) suggests 10 to 15 minutes, while[PatientNow](https://www.patientnow.com/resources/blog/ultimate-guide-appointment-scheduling-aesthetic-clinics) recommends five to ten between complex appointments. Neither cites data behind the number, so treat them as starting points and tune against your own day.


Service type Suggested buffer What the time covers


Neurotoxin or filler 10-15 min Charting units and lot, room reset, patient aftercare questions


New-patient consult 10-15 min Finishing the plan, treatment estimate, consent follow-up


Laser, microneedling, body contouring 15-20 min Device wipe-down, room turnover, settings log


IV or injection visit 5-10 min Line disposal, dose entry, restock


Quick recheck or suture removal 0-5 min Provider stays in the room; short note only


These are our suggested defaults, built from the ranges above and from how operators describe their days. Your own numbers should replace them within a month.


## Why Patients Still Book Into Gaps You Thought Were Protected


The most common cause is a service that holds no time at all. If a follow-up or recheck is saved with a duration of zero minutes, the calendar shows a card but the system sees an empty interval, so the provider looks free and online booking offers the slot. One clinic we heard from had two such follow-ups spaced fifteen minutes apart; a patient self-scheduled a 20-minute injectable between them.


The second cause is overlap settings. A service flagged as bookable alongside others is allowed to share a provider's time, which is intentional for some visits and a trap for the rest. The third is plain human habit, where staff book "just a quick one" over a visible gap. Fixing all three starts with an audit of every service on your menu: duration above zero, cleanup set, overlap allowed only on purpose.


## Buffers and Online Booking


Online booking will fill every minute you leave unprotected, so the buffer has to be part of the service definition rather than a note to staff. A patient looking at your booking page at 10 pm does not know a provider needs 15 minutes to chart; the software has to know.


Two settings matter. First, each service needs a real duration and, where relevant, a cleanup length that the availability engine adds before showing slots. Second, services that staff schedule manually, such as rechecks, should either have a short real duration or be hidden from self-scheduling. For more on the booking-flow side, see our guide to[med spa online booking errors](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-booking-setup-errors) , and our[med spa waitlist guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-waitlist) for filling cancelled slots without breaking your buffers.


## When Double Booking Is the Right Call


Double booking is right when the first appointment contains dead time the provider cannot use for anything else. A prospect on a recent sales call described exactly this: an injection visit that includes a wait, during which a new-patient consult could run with another team member. Allowing that overlap for that one service pair recovers real capacity. Allowing it everywhere guarantees collisions.


Use a short test before enabling overlap on a service. Is there a second person or room for the second visit? Is the first patient's visit genuinely idle for at least the consult's length? Does the overlap stay out of online booking? If any answer is no, keep that service single-booked. Mobile and travel-based practices face a variant of the same problem, covered in our[mobile IV booking setup guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/mobile-iv-booking-setup-guide) , where travel buffers replace room turnover.


## How to Tune Buffers Over Time


Measure scheduled hours against treatment hours for one typical week, then move buffers in five-minute steps. If providers consistently finish early, the buffer is too generous and you are leaving bookable time on the table. If the last patient of the day waits regularly or charting slips to the evening, it is too tight.


Prospyr's guide puts the cost of empty slots at up to $150,000 a year, though it does not cite its source, so use it as a prompt to measure rather than a benchmark. A simple monthly check covers it: pull average overrun per provider, average idle gap per provider, and the share of visits that started more than five minutes late. Late starts are the better signal because patients notice them, and they are also tied to no-shows, which our[med spa no-show guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/how-to-reduce-med-spa-no-shows) covers in depth.


## Common Buffer Mistakes to Audit Before You Change Anything


Most buffer problems come from four settings left at their defaults. Walk the service menu once and look for each of them before you add a single minute.


- **Zero-minute services.** Rechecks, follow-ups and "check-in" visits saved with no length. They look harmless on the calendar and hold nothing.
- **One buffer for everything.** A flat 15 minutes after a recheck wastes a quarter of an hour, while 15 after a laser session may not be enough.
- **Buffer set on the provider, not the service.** A provider-level gap applies to every visit, including the ones that need none, and it is easy to forget it exists.
- **Overlap switched on as a default.** If new services are created with overlap allowed, the problem returns every time someone adds a treatment.


A practical order is to fix zero-minute services first, since that stops the worst collisions, then set cleanup on the three or four highest-volume treatments, then review overlap. Most clinics see the difference in the first week because the calendar stops looking open when it is not.


## Buffer Time and Staff Workload


Buffers are also a staffing decision. An injector with no buffer finishes notes late in the day, which is when errors in lot numbers and units creep in. Charting while the visit is fresh is the cheaper habit, and buffer time is what makes it possible. Clinics that pay injectors on production, as covered in the[injector commission structure guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-injector-commission-structure) , should note that long buffers can feel like lost earnings, so explain the reason and revisit the numbers with the team.


Rebooking at checkout also needs breathing room. If the front desk is rushed, the next appointment does not get scheduled, which hurts[patient retention and rebooking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) . A buffer that gives the desk two minutes per patient pays for itself here.

## Final Thoughts on Med Spa Appointment Buffer Time


Pick a default by service type, put it in the service settings rather than in staff memory, give every bookable service a real duration, and allow overlap only where a second person covers it. Then measure for a month and adjust by five minutes. ## Frequently Asked Questions


How much buffer time should a med spa add between appointments?


Most scheduling guides land between 5 and 15 minutes. Start at 10 to 15 minutes after injectables and consults that need charting, 15 to 20 after laser or room-intensive services, and none after quick follow-ups where the provider stays in the room. Then adjust against how late your day actually runs.


Should buffer time be added to the service length or set separately?


Set it separately when your software allows it. A separate cleanup or buffer field holds the calendar without changing what the patient sees, and your reports still show the true treatment length. Padding the service itself works as a fallback but hides real durations from your utilization numbers.


Why can patients book into a gap that looks too small?


Online booking only respects time that is actually reserved. A service with a zero-minute duration, or a visit that is marked as double-bookable, holds nothing on the provider's calendar, so the system treats the slot as free. Give every bookable service a real duration and review which services are allowed to overlap.


Should follow-up or recheck visits have a duration?


Yes. Even a five-minute check needs a real length, because a zero-minute service reserves no provider time. Patients can then self-book into the same slot. Either give the service a short duration or remove it from online booking and let the front desk schedule it.


Is it ever fine to double book a provider?


Sometimes. A new-patient consult can run while an injector waits on numbing or while another patient sits through a short post-treatment observation. Allow overlap only for named services, and only with a second staff member or room covering the second visit. Never allow it as a blanket setting.


How do I know if my buffers are too long?


Compare scheduled hours to treatment hours for a typical week. If providers finish early most days, shorten the buffer by five minutes. If the last patient of the day regularly waits or the team skips charting, lengthen it. Review the numbers monthly for the first quarter, then each season.
